#4894. Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing

The Ethereum Foundation has doubled the size of its protocol security team and made strengthening Ethereum's cryptography its highest priority, warning that artificial intelligence could undermine the mathematical foundations of the network before quantum computers get powerful enough to do so.

"The EF has been planning mitigations to the threat posed by quantum computers," Kev Wedderburn wrote in a blog post published Monday, adding that "recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk."

For years, the crypto industry has worried about Q-Day—the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break the cryptography protecting digital assets. AI introduces a different problem: What if someone discovers a mathematical shortcut that makes such a machine unnecessary?

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Ethereum with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Bitcoin and Ethereum both rely on elliptic curve cryptography to authenticate transactions. Its security depends on mathematical problems that are relatively easy to solve in one direction but prohibitively difficult to reverse using known algorithms.

An AI capable of discovering substantially better algorithms could change that equation without requiring any breakthroughs in quantum hardware.

Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake raised this possibility in October, warning that existing signature schemes could become vulnerable within months rather than years under a worst-case scenario. He recommended that the industry start preparing for an orderly migration of funds to addresses whose public keys have never been exposed.

The Foundation's latest announcement comes just days after Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and Claude produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had remained unsolved since 1859.

The proof does not break Bitcoin or Ethereum's cryptography, but it illustrates how quickly AI is becoming useful in areas of mathematics previously considered beyond its capabilities.

The bug had survived roughly four years of scrutiny by cryptographers.

Ethereum's proposed solution involves moving away from elliptic curves and adopting hash-based cryptography. Hash functions turn data into fixed-length digital fingerprints that are designed to be extremely difficult to reverse, and their security relies on fewer structural mathematical assumptions than elliptic curve schemes.

Ethereum already depends on secure hash functions, making them an attractive foundation for its new security architecture.

The transition would affect how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how Ethereum verifies data submitted by layer-2 networks.

Developers are also pursuing formal verification, a technique that uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that software behaves according to its specifications. Ironically, AI could help accelerate that work.

The Foundation has been deploying AI agents against its own infrastructure since earlier this year, successfully identifying software vulnerabilities before malicious actors could exploit them.

The security overhaul comes at a cost. Ethereum developers will need to rethink some planned features, and larger cryptographic signatures could increase hardware requirements for people running their own nodes.

Development group Ethlabs has already withdrawn its proposal to introduce faster block production in the upcoming Hegotá upgrade, freeing up engineering resources to pursue an ambitious target of making Ethereum resistant to both threats in 2027.

The Foundation previously established December 2029 as its internal deadline for achieving quantum resistance across Ethereum's base layer. Drake proposed bringing that target forward to December 2028 at the recent Devcon conference in Mumbai.

The Foundation plans to reassess its timeline in January 2027, with developers already testing early implementations of the new cryptographic infrastructure.

#4887. Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits

Four months after attackers drained Bitcoin from compromised Coldcard hardware wallets, the device’s maker has published a detailed autopsy of how a single configuration error went undetected for more than five years, slipping past at least 15 separate security reviews before thieves exploited it.

The postmortem, released Monday by manufacturer Coinkite and modeled on an NTSB accident report, confirms the core failure when the exploit surfaced in July: from March 2021 through July 2026, Coldcard firmware generated wallet seeds using a software pseudo-random number generator, MicroPython’s Yasmarang, instead of the device’s intended hardware random-number generator.

The result was seeds with roughly 40 to 72 bits of effective randomness rather than the 128-bit target, weak enough for attackers to regenerate private keys offline and steal funds without ever touching a device.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The new report’s most revealing section is its accounting of why the flaw hid for so long.

Coinkite documented at least 15 independent review efforts between 2021 and 2026, including two paid third-party audits, physical-security work by Ledger Donjon, and even an AI-assisted firmware review that produced 85 findings. None caught it.

As the report puts it, every check “answered a nearby question rather than the critical one”: release checks confirmed the hardware-RNG code was present, but not that seed generation actually reached it, and statistical tests couldn’t distinguish the defective generator’s output from a properly seeded one.

A safeguard meant to reject the faulty configuration, a guard in the underlying libNgU code, simply didn’t work.

The scale of losses remains murky. Coinkite said it has received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 accounts, roughly 0.21% of its estimated user base, while Galaxy Research has attributed more than 8,600 addresses to the theft. The company cautions that those figures count different things and can’t be combined into a victim total.

One thread running through the report is the role of AI. Coinkite notes the first thefts began just two days after the Kimi K3 model’s full weights were released, calling AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution.”

It also documents how, after the flaw went public, the Bitcoin Red Team used Kimi K3 to run a 108-hour multi-model sweep that flagged nearly 8,000 candidate findings across 501 Bitcoin projects, underscoring how AI has upended the economics of vulnerability hunting.

Coinkite has since rebuilt its seed generation, adding mandatory user entropy, multiple hardware sources, and build-time and boot-time checks, with an independent review by Keylabs concluding the defect is “fully closed” in current standard firmware.

But no update repairs seeds already created on affected devices; those users must migrate to new ones. The report ends with a plea to whoever holds the stolen Bitcoin: return it.

“Some victims lost life-changing amounts, and returning the funds is the only action that can directly reduce that harm,” the company said.

#4885. Jade Cargill Was a Basketball Player Before the WWE. Here’s What Changed Everything

The 34-year-old wrestling superstar stops byThe Huddle ahead of her appearance on Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28th.

Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade says that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

“I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”

Despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she says.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

Jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

“I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”

Jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she says. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

“I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she says. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

“I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade says. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”

As a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she says. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”

And when a new opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she says. “And look at me now.”

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

To truly give these recommendations on the best storage beds, I featured options that include a variety of price points, storage features, designs, and more to guide you on your own shopping journey. Read more on the key factors other writers and I kept in mind below:

Delivery and Assembly: The last thing you want is to wait months for your bed frame to help you organize (and elevate) your space. We selected options that offer reasonable shipping windows (usually within one month from placing your order to its arrival at your home) as well as white glove delivery to help set up the storage bed in your desired room, or a frame simple enough to assemble yourself.

Design: A big passion of ours at AD is finding furniture that is not only functional but is also not an eyesore. We skipped clunky bed frames and included pieces that can sit comfortably anywhere in modern and minimalist bedrooms and beyond.

Size: Our editors tested a mix of queen and king sizes, and prices in this story reflect queens. We looked for picks that come in a range of sizes to accommodate any space. Keep in mind that storage beds often have features like pull-out drawers and lift-up bases, so be sure to measure your space and compare it to your desired storage bed's dimensions to ensure the bed can open properly in your bedroom.

Storage Features: The storage bed you select should align with your space. If you're tight on floor space, consider a storage bed that lifts up. If you have low ceilings, consider a storage bed that has drawers underneath.

Durability: We tested storage beds by sleeping on them night after night, taking notice of any factors like creakiness or wobbliness. We also looked for options with high-quality materials like fine upholstery and solid wood that are designed to last.

Price: Storage beds run from a few hundred dollars to well over $2,000, and our picks span that whole range. While the price isn't always the biggest indicator of quality, materials like bouclé and solid wood are usually found in more high-end storage beds.

What Are the Different Types of Storage Beds?

Lift-up beds: Also called an "ottoman bed," this is a model where the mattress base lifts up with the aid of gas struts (pressurized cylinders that do most of the lifting for you), which retailers often call hydraulic lifts. This typically offers the most room out of the storage bed options.

Drawer beds: Fairly self-explanatory: drawers (either under, alongside, or at the foot of the bed) are this frame’s storage approach.

Headboard storage beds: A headboard storage bed draws from mid-century styles, where built-in shelves or nightstands create storage opportunities. This is a good option if what you need to store is also aesthetically pleasing.

Cubby beds: Instead of drawers, these cubbies are open shelving solutions underneath the bed frame, particularly suitable for holding books if you’re looking for a stylish way to create a bedroom library.

What’s a “Hydraulic Lift” in a Storage Bed?

When your storage bed has interior storage (in other words, when you lift the mattress base upward to access its storage), it needs a lift mechanism to make it possible for you to lift the bed without breaking your back, and to keep the slatted frame upright while you lift your items in and out. Most use gas struts, though you'll often see them sold as hydraulic. If your storage bed has interior storage and no lift, you will collapse yourself and ultimately be pancaked by your own sleep-and-store investment.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Storage Beds?

A good storage bed, in our opinion, doesn't look like a storage bed. It looks like a regular bed. It's crafted from, ideally, kiln-dried hardwood, it has a slatted base so you don't need to bother with a box spring, and it has non-sticky drawers (thank you, Thuma) or a lift mechanism to help with the lifting of interior storage (thank you, Saatva). Look for a solid wood base, linen upholstery, and invest in some vacuum-sealed bags. I live by these.

You're primarily searching for durability and space in storage bed models. Look for frames made from solid wood since this type of material is typically sturdy and long-lasting. A lift mechanism makes storage more accessible without back-breaking exercises. While upholstered beds are a popular favorite, make sure what lies beneath the textile is also going to stand the test of time.

#4881. Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code

Anthropic is automating another part of software engineering: the process of deciding whether the code an AI writes is actually good enough to use.

The company introduced Claude Ship on Monday, a collection of AI agents capable of reviewing software changes, fixing errors, and approving code according to rules established by development teams.

Under certain configurations, software changes can make their way into a company's codebase without a human reading a single line of code.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

AI coding tools have become so good at producing software that reviewing it has become a bottleneck. Developers who previously spent hours writing a feature can now generate several in that time, but someone still has to check whether those changes work without breaking something else.

Anthropic is experiencing that problem itself. The company says Claude already writes most of the code produced by its Claude Code team.

Claude Ship combines three tools, each responsible for a different stage of the process. The first, Code Review, examines proposed changes against the existing codebase, using multiple agents to find potential bugs and verify each other's findings.

PR Steward, the second tool, makes the necessary corrections when automated tests fail or reviewers identify problems. It documents its modifications and provides instructions for reversing them, allowing developers to intervene if necessary.

The third tool, Claude Approvals, decides whether the proposed changes satisfy the company's approval policies. According to Anthropic's technical documentation, repositories configured for automatic merging can incorporate changes without anyone manually approving them.

The ability to delegate code reviews to AI is particularly attractive in the age of vibe coding, where developers—and increasingly people with little programming experience—build software by describing what they want in natural language.

But having an AI double-check another AI's work doesn't necessarily eliminate their shared weaknesses. A human programmer and a language model might approach a problem differently, whereas two agents powered by similar models could overlook the same flawed assumption.

A peer-reviewed study published earlier this year found that models from OpenAI and Anthropic performed slightly better at identifying and repairing security vulnerabilities in human-written code than in AI-generated code.

AI-assisted software development has already produced some expensive mistakes. In April, a startup founder reported that a coding agent running Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his company's production database and its volume-level backups through a single API call.

Anthropic's own experience with automated code reviews illustrates a different problem: AI agents can get stuck correcting each other. In one instance, according to an October engineering report, a proposed software change went through more than 50 rounds of automated reviews and corrections overnight before its author intervened.

The company nevertheless reported encouraging internal results. The number of merged changes more than doubled between June and September, while the proportion of changes that had to be reversed fell by more than 40%.

Those results came from a broader review process that retained human oversight for sensitive modifications, rather than a fully autonomous system. Changes to documentation can pass without human approval at Anthropic, whereas particularly risky modifications require two people to sign off.

“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it,” Anthropic's engineers wrote.

Whether other companies adopt equally restrictive policies is up to them. Claude Ship allows administrators to determine which parts of their software require human supervision and which decisions they are comfortable delegating to an AI.

The service is available for GitHub repositories on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, with charges based on token consumption. For now, Anthropic recommends running its automated approval system in observation mode, letting the AI demonstrate what it would have approved before giving it the authority to do so.

#4879. Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

The six-week postpartum checkup was never meant to be about fitness.

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that new moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.)

The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually says, and how to approach working out in this new chapter of life.

In many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport says. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”

These traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an important medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

The first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering says. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

To come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.)

Based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here

Pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport says. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport says. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport says. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

At the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” says Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”

For some new moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”

In fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye says. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!)

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, says Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you quickly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

There can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

And if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

Amy is a freelance writer and editor who covers health, fitness, and lifestyle topics—with a focus on practical advice that fits into real life. She previously worked as deputy fitness editor at SELF, and is both an ACE-certified personal trainer and a ProNatal pre and postnatal fitness specialist. Her work has been published in Women’s Health, Men’s Health, SELF, Wondermind, HGTV, Outside, REAL SIMPLE, The New York Times for Kids, and more. Amy lives in central New York where she spends her off-hours chasing after her two kids, digging into backyard gardening projects with her husband, and creatively squeezing at-home workouts into her schedule as often as she can.

#4876. OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release

Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly concerned that their companies' most advanced AI models may never be safe enough for public release, according to a Tuesday report by Axios citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions.

Some researchers believe the technical problems can eventually be solved. Others reportedly want the companies to stop training more intelligent models altogether.

The report comes two days after Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned that humanity might be approaching a point where it can no longer effectively supervise artificial intelligence. Wang argued that decisions made over the next year could determine whether humans retain control over increasingly autonomous, self-improving AI systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

His warning followed Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's announcement that an unreleased version of Claude had helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had frustrated researchers for 167 years.

The same intellectual abilities that make these models so valuable for scientific research are making them harder to supervise. A model capable of spotting something that generations of mathematicians missed could conceivably spot weaknesses in a safety system that its developers overlooked.

One of the biggest problems facing AI researchers involves reinforcement learning, a training technique that rewards models for successfully completing tasks. It's largely responsible for the impressive reasoning abilities of modern AI systems, but it can also teach them to cheat.

Researchers call this reward hacking. A model might, for example, manipulate the software responsible for grading its work instead of actually solving the problem it was assigned.

Anthropic encountered a version of this problem in February, when researchers reversed three days of training on Claude Mythos Preview after discovering undesirable behaviors. An internal review later flagged more than 10% of its active training environments for problems that included opportunities for cheating and incorrectly configured tasks.

Another problem involves chain-of-thought monitoring, which allows researchers to inspect the intermediate reasoning an AI generates before producing an answer or taking an action. Some unreleased models are increasingly capable of obscuring that reasoning or generating misleading explanations that satisfy their monitors.

In other words, the explanation researchers receive may no longer accurately reflect how the model arrived at its decision.

OpenAI has already experienced the real-world consequences of inadequate containment. The company acknowledged that an internal research model was primarily responsible for compromising AI development platform Hugging Face while pursuing a difficult task.

Keeping the smartest models away from ChatGPT and Claude users would therefore address only part of the problem.

“Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.

OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed Sunday that AI developers agree on common limits to model development, based partly on perplexity—a mathematical measure of how accurately a model predicts subsequent pieces of text, with lower scores indicating better predictions.

Pachocki argues that companies should agree not to cross certain thresholds until researchers develop more effective ways of monitoring AI behavior. He estimates that AI-assisted research could substantially accelerate the development of new models as early as 2027.

Getting competing companies to voluntarily slow down could prove particularly difficult, especially as investors expect returns on the enormous amounts of money pouring into AI infrastructure. Anthropic itself raised more than $81 billion when it went public last week.

OpenAI said last week that it would suspend training or withhold models again if they failed to satisfy its safety requirements. Anthropic has separately committed to publishing a policy proposal on independent AI evaluators by December 15, followed by a framework addressing the pace of AI development by January 15, 2027.

#4873. Take-Two Hits GTA 6 PC Port Leonida With DMCA, Taking Down 3,007 GitHub Repos

Take-Two Hits GTA 6 PC Port Leonida With DMCA, Taking Down 3,007 GitHub Repos

Take-Two Interactive has used a copyright takedown notice to remove Leonida, one of the most prominent projects attempting to port the leaked Xbox build of Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC, along with thousands of copies of its code.

GitHub published a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notice from Take-Two's IP Enforcement Team on Tuesday. Because the publisher alleged that all or most of the project's forks infringed to the same extent as the original, GitHub said it processed the takedown against the entire network of 3,007 repositories.

The notice clears up why the project disappeared on Monday. Its GitHub page had shown an error page rather than a DMCA notice, so it was initially unclear whether it had been removed by its creator or by Take-Two.

The project described itself as "a native PC recompilation of the Xbox version of Grand Theft Auto 6." Take-Two said it reproduced copyrighted elements of the game and was a derivative work, breaching Rockstar's terms of service, which bar users from decompiling, reverse engineering or creating derivative works from its games.

Leonida did not include the leaked game files itself. Instead, its instructions told users to supply their own Xbox Series files.

Take-Two dismissed that approach. Stolen files from an Xbox Series build of the game were publicly distributed on November 20, 2026, and Leonida's repository opened the following day, it said.

"The instruction to 'bring your own files' attempts to shift the responsibility for supplying files to the user and to make it seems as if this is a general-purpose project," Take-Two wrote. "This is intentionally misleading."

The timing and the project's "explicit focus" on Grand Theft Auto showed the files users needed were the leaked ones, and that its developers knew it, Take-Two added. It asked GitHub to disable the repository and all its forks.

Take-Two has made the same argument before. On November 18, GitHub published four Take-Two notices against unofficial ports of GTA V to mobile devices, Macs and web browsers, three of which told users to supply their own game files. In each, Take-Two said such disclaimers "do not automatically shield" developers from secondary copyright liability when they knowingly facilitate infringement.

The project's pseudonymous creator also posted a screenshot of a Discord notice saying his server had broken the platform's rules on copyright infringement, limiting his access to servers until November 30, 2026.

He later tweeted that he was no longer working on the project "because of T2," but that "there are and always will be more projects." On Wednesday, he told followers to ignore his earlier posts, adding: "Something's coming soon."

Ignore my other posts. Something’s coming soon 👀

— NotRexed (@ItsNotRexed) November 25, 2026

The takedown follows the release of the build's main executable by leaker Cyberleek on Monday. Cyberleek had promised to release the file if the CYBERLEEK meme coin reached a $15 million market cap. The token fell short, but Cyberleek released the file anyway, and porting projects expected a playable version within days.

Take-Two has pursued the leaks for months, subpoenaing Discord and Microsoft, which owns GitHub, in August for data that could help identify Cyberleek. Rockstar has not announced a PC version of GTA 6.

#4870. You Know Animal-Print Rugs, But Do You Know Animal Pictorials? (2026)

The oldest known pile rug—pulled from a frozen tomb in Siberia in 1949—features a procession of 24 fallow deer and a parade of men on horseback. Some 2,500 years after its creation, animal illustrations are making their way back onto the floor. A serpent coils through the Snake and Pomegranate rug by Christopher Farr and Studio Shamshiri in Lucy Hale’s Los Angeles home, and a Tibetan tiger stretches across Demi Lovato’s modern farmhouse and Ethan Cook’s SoHo loft. These aren’t spots or stripes standing in for a neutral—they’re meant to be noticed and discussed. “Animal print is a texture; an animal motif is a story,” says AD100 designer Pavitra Rajaram, who recently designed Bahaar, an animal-themed rug in her Majnun collection for Jaipur Living. “I think people are tired of decoration that says nothing and are looking for objects that carry meaning.”

Rajaram is describing a literal animal rug, also known as an animal pictorial. These playful floor coverings often feature a bucolic scene of several animals or a single animal form woven into the textile, and they come in styles ranging from avant-garde and surrealist to Art Deco and folk-inspired.

“What we’re seeing now is a shift toward rugs where the whole animal is part of the design and has a role in the composition,” says Kerri Anne Besse, design director at rug brand Tumble. “The oversized, blown-up animal print feels dated.”

As for styling, Sophie Salata, head of brand at Vinterior, recommends that designers let the pictorials stand on their own. “I’d be inclined to treat the rug almost as a piece of art, allowing it to become a focal point rather than trying to make everything around it match,” she says. Pamela Marshall, creative director at artisanal rug brand Patterson Flynn, agrees with this approach: These designs are more than backdrops.

Reformation's nine-piece rug collection with Les Éditions de Tapis includes depictions of cats, swans, and tigers.

Recently, brands have been launching their own interpretations of animal pictorials. Last week, Reformation launched its first-ever home collection, a collaboration with Les Éditions de Tapis that features hand-drawn swans and cats. At Milan Design Week this year, Fornasetti launched a surrealist-inspired line of rugs with CC-Tapis depicting slithering serpents from the luxury designer’s archive. A few months earlier, Ruggable released its collaboration with Scalamandré to bring the upscale design house’s iconic zebras to more homes. And in October 2025, Nordic Knots launched its Swedish Grace collection, including the Grace 03 Fauna rug, which shows a wildlife scene. Looking further back, Beni’s serpent rugs have been a designer favorite since 2020.

One of the earlier examples of literal animal rugs is a collection between longstanding collaborators Patterson Flynn and AD100 designers Charlap Hyman & Herrero. It grew from a one-off rug into a full collection of graphic natural-and-black silhouettes that launched in 2018 and continues to expand. “Areas of inspiration for these come from Calder’s simplified animal forms, the surrealists’ play on scale, and 17th-century cabinets of curiosity, to name a few,” says Marshall, who credits Hyman’s “encyclopedic” design references for the originality. We would be remiss not to mention Diane von Furstenberg’s long-running collaboration with the Rug Company, which has been producing the iconic Climbing Leopard rug since 2005.

Rugs from Charlap Hyman & Herrero x Patterson Flynn’s collaboration.

The Rug Company x Diane von Furstenberg Climbing Leopard rug in emerald.

These rugs’ rich history might be part of their renewed appeal. Animals have been a subject for as long as people have made pictures. The oldest known figurative cave painting—found in Indonesia and dated to at least 51,200 years ago—shows a wild pig with three human figures.

“Animals have shaped our textiles and rugs for longer than we think,” says Bella Valenzia, founder of Pelican House, pointing out that animal forms have appeared in tapestries and wall coverings, and as functional home objects, such as pelt and hide rugs used for warmth and comfort, since the earliest days of humankind. “We like to think it is part of a wider return to folk-inspired, storytelling textiles, with a sense of nostalgia,” she adds. Pelican House’s rug Frith references the old English countryside, where horses have long been at the heart of rural life.

Various animals, real and mythical, carry their own significance across cultures, and their meaning can deeply influence a home’s design. For example, a pictorial of a lion, which signifies power in certain cultures, adds a very different element to a space than a fish, which can signify good luck, notes Jahanshah “Josh” Nazmiyal of Rug & Kilim. Veronica Renton, senior vintage and antiques specialist at 1stDibs, adds that peacocks often signal nobility and immortality.

Plenty of designers still reach for the originals: While the contemporary versions of these rugs are having a moment, their earlier counterparts remain relevant. “I particularly love antique Tibetan tiger rugs and Persian and Chinese rugs featuring guardian lions, dragons, and all manner of mythical beasts,” says Tiffany Duggan, founder of Studio Duggan.

The Tiger Rug by Studio Ashby in Sophie Ashby’s former home in London.

Where these rugs live in the home is likewise important. Naturally, the pieces work well in spaces that are meant to be playful, like nurseries and children’s rooms. For example, in this garden apartment designed by Rebecca Benichou and Florence Jallet of Batiik Studio, the Toulemonde Bochart Lion rug brings a spot of levity to a windowless craft room. In the bedroom of Kate Upton and Justin Verlander’s daughter, Genevieve, designed by John Ruggiero, the Doing Goods Blooming Black Bear Rug provides a spot of whimsy. For double the fun, designer Olivia Song put two animal rugs, the Doing Goods Pinky Lion and Pinky Leopard, in her nephew’s room in this Sag Harbor beach home.

That said, these rugs work in more adult spaces, too. “In the [primary] bedroom of one of our London projects, we used the beautiful Snake and Pomegranate rug,” says Duggan. “I love the way the snake weaves its way around the bed, creating a focal point and bringing a little humor and unexpected character to an otherwise calm space.”

Designer Rayman Boozer from Apartment 48 has a rug with a large tiger on it from the Rug Company in his own home. “Animal motifs can sometimes feel juvenile, but there’s something refreshing about bringing that sense of playfulness into a sophisticated space,” he says.

Rayman Boozer’s home, featuring an Apartment 48 tiger rug.

Steven Loloi, co-principal at Loloi, agrees. Speaking of Loloi’s Roam collection that launched last month and features cheetahs, zebras, elephants, and giraffes in neutral colors, he highlights the surprising versatility of the pieces, which he says can fit just as nicely in a bedroom or living room as in a lounge or den. “I think we’re seeing people become more confident in their design choices and a little less concerned with playing it safe,” he says. “Why not have a leopard or zebra in your living room?”

It’s worth noting that these rugs aren’t for everyone, and some designers avoid any type of animal rug because of the hunting culture they reference. Others, though, embrace them as a way to reimagine humanity’s relationship to animals and commit to living better by them.

Rajaram's Bahaar rug does just that with its contemporary expression of 'shikargahs,' the enclosed forests where kings hunted at leisure, which are celebrated in Iranian and Mughal design. “Instead of being chased, the animals are in harmony with each other, frolicking freely in the forest. It’s a celebration of coexistence rather than conquest,” she says. The Charlap Hyman & Herrero x Patterson Flynn collection had a similar ambition: “Our Tigre and Oso nod to traditional hide floor coverings; they give you the drama of the trophy rug without the trophy,” notes Marshall.

On the surface, the return of these animal-forward rugs might have looked like a change in aesthetics, but it’s really much more anthropological. “We have always gravitated toward pieces with animals, and even in modern production, history is repeating itself,” says Nazmiyal. Some 2,500 years after their first spotting, these animal-clad rugs are back home.

#4865. Hyperliquid Leads Altcoin Losses as Bitcoin Slips Below $59K

Hyperliquid Leads Altcoin Losses as Bitcoin Slips Below $59K

Hyperliquid's HYPE token led crypto's latest leg down on Wednesday, as one of the exchange's most profitable traders shut down its operations there.

HYPE fell 8.2% over 24 hours to $57.86, the steepest drop among the 20 largest cryptocurrencies by market cap, and is down 15.8% over the past week, according to Decrypt data. Bitcoin slipped 1.7% over the same period to $58,801, and Ethereum lost 2.4%, extending a sell-off that has spread across risk assets.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short HYPE with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Abraxas Capital has withdrawn its remaining funds from Hyperliquid and closed its entire book, almost two years after it started trading there, pseudonymous onchain analyst MLM said on Telegram on Tuesday.

The firm traded $13.4 billion on Hyperliquid and made $530 million, including at least $67 million from funding payments, according to MLM. The positions were one leg of a market-neutral strategy for its Elysium Global Arbitrage Fund, the analyst said.

Two Hyperliquid accounts labeled as Abraxas Capital on analytics platform Hyperdash have recorded combined all-time profits of more than $550 million, and now hold just over $5,000 between them, Hyperdash data shows. On Tuesday, the two accounts unstaked about 219,000 HYPE, worth roughly $12.7 million at current prices, and sent it elsewhere.

"With HYPE, upcoming token unlocks could be adding extra pressure," Eric Andersson, co-founder of Byrrgis, told Decrypt. "Altcoins tend to get hit even harder in these situations."

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $231.6 million in net outflows on Tuesday, their sixth consecutive day of withdrawals, according to SoSoValue data. Outflows over those six trading days total $2.6 billion.

That takes November's net outflows to $4.94 billion, surpassing June 2026's $4.51 billion as the funds' worst month since they launched in January 2024. Total net assets stand at $72 billion.

Andersson pointed to ETF outflows, uncertainty over interest rates, liquidations and weaker sentiment across financial markets as drivers of Bitcoin's decline.

Options traders have turned increasingly bearish. Over the past week, 1.7 put options, which pay out when prices fall, changed hands for every call on a seven-day average, the most since June 2022, Glassnode said in its weekly report. Measured by open interest, the ratio is at its highest since May 2021.

Bitcoin is back at its summer lows near $60K, and stocks are also in a downtrend.

BTC gave back the whole NVIDIA rally in less than six hours, an indication of severe relative weakness.

More on capitulation and leverage in this week's Week On-chain. https://t.co/GwEUc1pqHW

— glassnode (@glassnode) November 24, 2026

Such readings do not always mark a bottom. In June 2022, a similar reading coincided with a price low, but the bear market's final low was still five months away, while the open interest peak in April 2021 came near a market top, Glassnode noted.

Glassnode also said options dealers are "short gamma" between $58,000 and $64,000, meaning their hedging requires them to sell as prices fall and buy as they rise, which can make moves in either direction larger. Just outside that range, their hedging would slow a move, the firm said.

Glassnode's report found that Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX.

A clearer outlook on interest rates and renewed ETF inflows could help bring stability back to the market, Andersson said.

#4863. Want Headphones Built for Real Workouts? These 9 Survived Runs, Jumps, and Gym-Bag Chaos

Headphones that can handle as much as you can.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout. As a fitness writer and longtime distance runner, I’ve seen firsthand how the right headphones can make or break a workout. And I’ve worked my way through a range of workout headphones before I found the ones I don’t want to be without.

I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run. (I never recovered it.) I’ve also discovered that some headphones are better for certain types of workouts over others. Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

The Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

It has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

It also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

When I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. Battery life could be better for all-day wear, but it’s good for workouts (assuming you’re not working out all day). I hit the gym after work, and the power is always drained after an eight-hour day. On the flip side, it’s easy to juice up in 15 minutes with the charging case (it offers up to 30 hours of battery life per charge). To fully restore the battery, make sure to charge overnight. Read More: Best Fitness Trackers

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are an absolute treasure. I own a lot of headphones, but the sound quality always keeps me coming back for more. The over-ear design completely covers my ears, providing A-grade noise cancellation at prime-time hours.

The sound is immersive with balanced, deep bass that doesn’t feel piercing—an issue with lower-quality headphones I tested. I blast my tunes at full volume when getting in the zone, and I never feel uncomfortable.

They look bulky, but looks can be deceiving. They never budge, even when speed walking at an incline or doing fast-paced plyometric drills. I’ve worn it during box jumps and ice skaters, and it stayed put.

Just note it’s not water resistant for intense cardio like spinning and running, where you’ll work up a sweat—although the plush padding rimming the headband and ear cups can easily be wiped clean.

Like the Apple AirPods Pro 3, I have to charge it daily in the included case, so make sure to keep the cable on hand for quick power-ups.

Read More: The Best Slim Fitness Trackers

If you really just can’t with the possibility of your earbuds falling out, but still want a compact option, Dr. Dre delivered just what you need: the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. It has hooks that seamlessly glide over the ears, ensuring a proper fit that stays put. And compared to the previous iteration that launched six years ago, it’s now smaller and lighter, and shares many of the same features as the AirPods Pro 3 (Apple does own Beats, after all), including active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring through the Beats app.

I’ve put it to the test during long runs, sprints, low-impact biking, and strength training. The verdict? It performs as sleekly as it looks. The sound is crisp and rich, while the bass is heavy without being overbearing.The sweat resistance is a notch below AirPods with an IPX4 rating, meaning it can withstand light rain but can’t be submerged. I’ve gotten caught in the rain one too many times while wearing these—yet, the sound quality is still the same as it was straight out of the box. And battery life is actually slightly better than AirPods, offering up to 45 hours with the charging case.However, this pair feels more uncomfortable than the Apple AirPods Pro 3. The material feels a little too hard for my liking. If you plan on walking or running for hours, the best overall is the way to go.

The last thing you want is uncomfortable headphones when in the midst of PRing your next barbell squat. Working out is tough enough, so having a pair that’s übersoft will take away some of the pain. Meet the Sony WH-1000XM6—a splurge that’s worth the investment.

Thick foam on the ear cups feels like lying on a pillow, while it also seals sound better for superior noise cancellation. The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

The headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

If you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A big draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

The earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an issue with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

These earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

If you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

The silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an issue since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

For example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

#4862. Florida Man Jailed for Using AI to Pose as Streamer N3ON in $260K Crypto Scam

Florida Man Jailed for Using AI to Pose as Streamer N3ON in $260K Crypto Scam

A Port St. Lucie, Florida, man has been sentenced to 47 months in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate popular streamer N3ON and con a meme coin project's organizers out of roughly $260,000 in crypto.

David Anthony Sanchez, 36, who also went by "Dave the Jewler" and other aliases, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Melissa Damian after pleading guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida said on Tuesday. He was also ordered to pay restitution to his victims.

A Port St. Lucie man was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate a popular online streamer and deceive investors in a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that caused approximately $260,000 in losses. The case serves as a warning that… pic.twitter.com/4DZnaiaPNt

— US Attorney's Office Southern District of Florida (@USAO_SDFL) November 24, 2026

According to court records, Sanchez set up online accounts made to look as though they belonged to N3ON, and contacted the organizers of a crypto meme coin project while posing as both the streamer and his representative.

He signed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent the organizers an AI-generated voice recording that mimicked the streamer, falsely confirming that N3ON would endorse, promote and take part in the project, prosecutors said. Believing the deal was real, the organizers sent about $260,000 in crypto to accounts Sanchez controlled.

Sanchez then converted much of the crypto into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to hide where the money came from and who owned it, and spent it on himself, according to prosecutors. The press release did not name the meme coin project.

"The defendant exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate the trust of unsuspecting victims and deprive them of their money," Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in a statement.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short SOL with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The case is a small example of a fast-growing type of crypto fraud. Impersonation scams grew more than 1,400% year on year in 2025, driven in part by AI tools, as crypto scam losses reached a record $17 billion, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated in January.

AI deepfakes of government officials, billionaires and celebrities accounted for 40% of high-value crypto frauds in 2024, according to a report from crypto exchange Bitget. Earlier this month, the Justice Department said North Korean hackers had stolen more than $400 million in crypto over 18 months through a scheme it calls "FaceStealer," which uses recorded webcam footage and deepfake videos to impersonate victims' trusted contacts on video calls. The same tactics have been used to target crypto workers.

Legislation aimed at the problem has stalled. The AI Fraud Deterrence Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Neal Dunn (R-FL) in November 2025, would raise penalties for AI-assisted fraud.

AI-assisted money laundering, one of the charges Sanchez pleaded guilty to, would carry fines of up to $1 million or three times the value of the transaction, alongside up to 20 years in prison. The bill has not advanced beyond the House Judiciary Committee.
