It achieves this thanks to its signature Helion Superfoam midsole, which sets itself apart with a construction that blends rigid, stable sections with flexible foam. This combination of materials provides the perfect balance of cushioning and energy return, giving you a bouncy, lightweight feel when your foot hits the pavement. The result is a soft, natural ground feel, rather than an overly bouncy cushioning experience. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). It’s her all-time favorite race shoe—she even ran a half-marathon in it.

According to Accardi, the shoe feels firm but still has enough flexibility that her running gait isn’t impacted. The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. Even when her legs feel like they’re about to give out, these shoes pick her right back up. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. The CloudTec system, which uses air pockets in the midsole (the layer between the insole and the outsole), to create the shoe’s cushiony feel, propels me forward with every step, kind of like walking on a trampoline. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy T-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

One thing to note, though, is the sole wears down fast, which we found to be disappointing, especially given that price tag. Accardi says the Clifton 10 has a better tread thanks to its thicker outsole designed for high-friction.

Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!). That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it literally feels like walking on pillows.

With the most cushioning of any shoe on this list (and the most cushioning Brooks offers), it’s perfect for those who need extra support. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says it has extra plush, foamy cushioning, but even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s incredibly stable thanks to Brooks’ signature Guardrails technology, which is a broad base with two pieces of foam on either side of the heel. It reduces the rolling of the foot both inward and outward, so it cradles your foot in place without messing with your stride. According to Appleton, this combination is great for those with higher arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel an ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options (huge win!).

During testing, I did notice that there was some wear and tear on the shoe pretty early on (it had only been a few months of use). The material on the upper of the shoe wore out pretty quickly. While this knocked it down a few points in my book, its supreme comfort still kept this kick at the very top of my list. Plus, I love how many fun colors the shoe comes in—because running and walking should be fun, right?!

The Hoka Clifton 11 is a standout favorite among WH editors. After testing nearly every Hoka model, I can attest that the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar—just a smidge lighter and more springy. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly narrower, too, but it doesn’t feel tight or uncomfortable. I prefer the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Despite its lighter weight, it has a generous stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also find that the foam absorbs impact well. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never feel fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride feels smooth and natural whether I’m walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review

There’s nothing worse than slipping into an uncomfortable shoe after a tough run—that’s where the Alo Recovery Sneaker comes in. Designed to support tired feet, it features a structured sole and high-rebound foam insole that offers arch support and bounces back into place with each step. It makes every step feel stable, cushioned, and balanced. The second I put this pair on after a long run, my feet are instantly relaxed. I can’t say that about most of my other sneakers.

One of the biggest perks of this shoe? The traction is next-level, which is key for a recovery sneaker that’s meant to keep you comfortable and steady all day. Inside, the sock-like lining prevents your foot from sliding around. The thick ankle collar also helps stabilize the foot and provides extra support up the leg, keeping everything locked in place.

Style-wise, this sneaker goes with everything—sweats, shorts, jeans, leggings, you name it. That’s why I crowned it the best overall platform sneaker. After giving it a spin for a few weeks running around Manhattan, walking my dog around Long Island, and wearing it to and from workout classes, it's done the best job at keeping my feet pain-free compared to many other platform sneakers I've worn. The 1.5-inch platform is subtle but adds just the right amount of height to elongate my legs without being so tall that I feel unstable. Oh, and it’s super cute to boot. I’m a big fan of the Natural White colorway, which looks clean and classic, and pairs effortlessly with everything from sweatpants to denim.

Even if you’re not fresh off a run, it works for the office, errands, or a casual lunch. It’s hands down one of the most versatile (and most worn) shoes in my closet. My one con is that it feels a bit heavy and bulky, especially after a long day of wear.

Read more: Alo Recovery Mode Sneaker Review

I hadn't tried Asics until this year, and now it's my go-to shoe brand. Not only does its shoe have a streetwear vibe (I'm loving the bright yellow color with sweats and jeans), but they’re also some of the most comfortable shoes I’ve ever worn. In the UB9-S Gel Kayano 20s, the brand uses its signature gel cushioning technology, which features gel units placed in both the heel and forefoot of the shoe to absorb shock and provide a soft landing. This cushioning adapts to your foot’s movement, offering flexibility while reducing impact on your joints. Plus, the form-fitting upper keeps your foot locked in place, making it perfect for long runs, but stylish enough for everyday wear.

I wear this shoe everywhere—on runs, in the gym, and even to the office—and I get compliments virtually every single time I step out in it. The support is unmatched, the traction is solid, and it’s lightweight enough that I never feel weighed down. Plus, it breaks in fast (I wore it right out of the box), so there’s no awkward adjustment period. If you’re looking for a sneaker that can do it all while still looking cool, this is the one for you.

One con to note: It comes in some funky colors, so if you’re not into something bright and fun, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. I also wish it came in a wider version for those with wider feet and bunions.

We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” says WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

Now with a lighter weight and a lower heel-to-toe drop (6 mm compared to 9.5 mm), the shoe doesn’t weigh me down and puts less stress on the ankles and feet. I’m a big fan of the wider base for lifting and squatting because it makes my feet feel locked. The forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter add extra security, while the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

And post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. I recently wore this sneaker while traveling, and it kept my feet happy power walking through the airport and standing in long security and customs lines. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”

The fit is true to size, and while wide-size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, the wide outsole may feel too bulky during stair climbing or quick, dynamic moves.

Let me introduce you to my new favorite low-profile, fashion sneaker: the Puma Speedcat. It’s been making waves with style girls, and after testing it out for months, I can see why. This shoe pairs so well with any outfit, with a slim, almost ballet-flat silhouette that doesn’t clash with nicer pieces in my wardrobe. I even see celebs like Em Rata sport the Speedcat all the time, and they always make any streetwear ‘fit look so chic and cool.

Like the Samba, it has a pretty flat sole, but I actually find it more cushioned thanks to its EVA midsole, which has a lightweight, cushioned feel and shock-absorbing properties. This means I can walk around for longer without my feet aching. Plus, after wearing it on wet city streets, I’ve noticed it has better traction, which is a huge win.

The only downside? The fit is a little narrow, especially in the toe area. If you have wider feet, I’d definitely recommend sizing up.

Originally designed for indoor soccer, the Adidas Samba has become a cult-favorite sneaker that’s just as popular on the streets as it is on the field. At first glance, the Samba looks pretty flat, so I wasn’t expecting much in terms of comfort. But after logging hundreds of miles walking around the city, I was surprised by how well it supports my feet. The Samba uses a combination of synthetic leather for the upper and a rubber sole with a cushioned midsole for comfort. The cushioning is more subtle compared to high-performance running shoes, but it still provides a soft, supportive feel. Even without a ton of cushioning, I rarely experience discomfort, which is impressive for a sneaker this sleek. It runs narrow, especially for wide feet, and I recommend going a half size down, as it tends to run big—many with wider feet or bunions agree it’s not the best fit.

It’s a go-to for effortlessly cool outfits—you can wear it with jeans, dresses, slacks, or shorts and always look stylish. I own this shoe in two different colorways (it comes in so many different shades), and after wearing it with practically everything in my closet, I can confidently say it adds a sporty, trendy touch to any outfit.

One of Under Armour’s first-ever shoes, this kick is rooted in sport. But it’s gotten some essential upgrades since its launch, and it’s safe to say I’m hooked. Since 2009, it’s been updated with leather upper overlays to keep the foot supported and soft UA HOVR cushioning, made from soft EVA foam and rubber, which is engineered to store and release energy with each step, providing a bouncy, responsive feel that helps propel you forward. Out of all the shoes I’ve tried, this pair feels the most bouncy, which I know is an absolute essential for the runners and walkers out there that like that super thick underfoot feel. It also has a rocker shape to keep the foot in a forward motion for less energy exertion.

The UA Apparition also has a mesh upper for supreme breathability—I’ve worn it during HIIT workouts, runs, and walks and never feel like my feet are constricted or sweaty, but I still feel supported and balanced. With a sleek, minimalistic look, the Apparition pairs well with anything from gym gear to casual streetwear. The rubber outsole provides traction and durability, allowing for smooth transitions during both dynamic workouts and everyday use.

My one con? There are some fun colors available, but I wish there were more options to choose from.

When it comes to comfortable sneakers, cushioning should be your top priority—whether you’re walking, running, hitting the gym, or just running errands. Here are the cushioning levels you can expect to see in the shoes below:

As Women’s Health editors, we practically live in sneakers, so we know what it takes for a shoe to feel super comfortable. When I originally put together this list of the most comfortable sneakers in 2025, I spent over two years testing more than 50 pairs in every possible scenario—long and short walks, runs, HIIT workouts, full days out in NYC, travel days, and more. For this 2026 update, myself and other WH editors re-tested newer iterations of our favorite pairs to make sure they still meet our standards. I also sought advice from fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, as well as style contributor Lily Wohlner. We looked at everything from cushioning and stability to sizing, traction, and color options. And if a pair left our feet aching or uncomfortable, it didn’t make the cut. So you can trust that every sneaker on this list kept our feet happy all day long—even through our toughest workouts.

#4840. In This Seaside Rhode Island Family Home, the Interiors Have an Ever-Changing Color Palette Inspired by the Ocean

“It was like Frankenstein,” says the husband of the shingled postmodern house on Rhode Island’s rocky coast that he shares with his wife and their three young-adult children. Built by his father in the 1980s, the house occupies an extraordinary site overlooking the Atlantic ocean and an expansive marsh. But successive additions had left it architecturally disjointed. The Manhattan-based couple, fresh from updating a Litchfield County weekend retreat with AD PRO Directory designer James “Ford” Huniford, asked him to take another look. “We were thrilled to have him try to rethink this house for us,” says the wife, “which may have been easier in retrospect to just knock down.”

In a favorite sitting room, which Huniford reconfigured from a triangle into a rectangle, rattan Audoux-Minet armchairs and a custom sofa flanked by 1930s Kittinger pedestal tables wear cushions covered in a Colefax and Fowler chintz. The walls, clad in Scalamandré wallpaper, display 1950s ceramic plates from Italy’s Amalfi Coast, while an antique French chandelier hangs overhead. The coffee table is custom and the carpet is from Sacco. “I was impressed with [Ford’s] ability to take risks and do things that were different than he had done,” says the wife, pointing to the chintz fabric, “and we were very happy with the outcome.”

The French wicker barrel chair with a Jasper-covered cushion and a custom sofa, upholstered in Pierre Frey, complete the seating arrangement around a vintage coffee table. Layered beneath are rugs from Doris Leslie Blau and Sacco, the former a midcentury Scandinavian design. Rococo side tables each support a 1930s Camille Tharaud vase lamp, while the 1961 patinated-brass ceiling lights by Jacques Quinet are from Galerie Apaganthe.

Rather than impose a conventional beach-house aesthetic, Huniford sought to evoke the early-20th-century summer houses of New England while preserving the existing structure’s character. His references ranged from the work of architect Fred Lincoln Savage on Maine’s Mount Desert Island to Kilkare, a Victorian oceanfront estate in Wainscott, New York. New rooflines, structural bump-outs, covered porches, traditional divided-light windows, and detailing brought a sense of accumulated history, even as the house was winterized and its systems updated. Expanded interiors and improved flow were achieved with remarkably little change to the overall footprint. “To me,” says Huniford, “the luxury is in the detail of the craft.”

Garden-inspired Ferrick Mason wallpaper enlivens the jewel-box powder room, where a vintage pedestal sink is paired with a Samuel Heath faucet. Antique Italian sconces flank a vintage Italian mirror from Donzella, while a green 1970s pendant by Hans-Agne Jakobsson for Staff and a Rug & Kilim rug complete the space.

In the dining area, English whitewashed painted chairs upholstered in a Pierre Frey fabric surround a custom table draped with an antique coarse-linen buggy blanket and topped with Vallauris woven plates and a 1960s Émile Tessier cachepot. Above hangs a 19th-century Dutch brass chandelier from Brownrigg, while Josef Albers color case studies enliven the walls. “What I love about Ford is: I was like, ‘Are you sure that we should paint the walls yellow?’” the wife recalls of Huniford’s custom paint selection. “And he’s like, ‘I don’t know. This is a whole new world for me, but yeah, I think we should.’”

Inside, the designer took his cues from the wraparound vistas and shifting natural light, particularly during the summer months, when the family spends most of its time here. “The ocean can be dark black and then it can be blue and then it can be green,” says Huniford. “I love the sea. It’s such a magical thing.” That ever-changing palette informed rooms of relaxed refinement, where the mix includes English, French, and early American furnishings, many slipcovered in upholstery washed to achieve an effortlessly lived-in quality. “They don’t like clutter, and they don’t like fussiness,” Huniford notes of his clients. “They like function, and they love form.”

In the kitchen, striped wall covering by Maresca Textiles provides a lively backdrop for vintage opaline globe wall lights, Newport Brass plumbing fixtures, and a collection of vintage ceramics and tableware. A French bobbin chair is from Andrew Spindler Antiques & Design.

In a newly added pantry adjoining the dining area, new and vintage tabletop treasures include Tiffany & Co. salt and pepper mills, a stoneware pitcher by Bennington Potters, green Dieulefit glasses, and bowls from Paula Rubenstein.

The palette of another sitting room takes its cues from the nearby ocean. Braided-rattan lounge chairs by Henry Link, sourced at Brimfield and topped with cushions in a Décors Barbares fabric, flank an armless sofa with Christopher Farr–covered seat cushions and back cushions upholstered in a Fabricut textile. The coffee table, side table, and lamp are vintage; the ceiling fixture is by Schoolhouse, and the carpet is from Stark.

Yet there is plenty of playfulness beneath the restraint. Huniford introduced an unexpected palette and, in a first for both designer and clients, chintz. In the open-plan living, kitchen, and dining areas, where windows were left free of treatments, sea-glass-green doors complement wide-plank walls painted a buttery yellow. Colorful works by Josef Albers, a favorite of the husband and sourced by Huniford, provide a graphic counterpoint near a dining table surrounded by whitewashed chairs and draped with an antique rough-linen buggy cover. In an adjacent sitting room, rattan furniture brightened by cushions in a radiant Colefax & Fowler floral take center stage. “I never thought in a million years that I’d have chintz in my house,” admits the wife, “but it now happens to be my favorite fabric.”

A dreamy layering of florals defines the primary bedroom, from Temple Studio wallpaper and a headboard and bed skirt in Bennison Fabrics textiles to a Matouk bedspread and pillowcases and a blanket from The Company Store. A vase and lamp from Huniford’s vintage stock sit atop a side table from Fernyhough Antiques.

An English neoclassical mahogany desk by Kittinger, sourced on Chairish, is where the husband prefers to work while taking in ocean views. The desk chair and lamp are vintage, while a dhurrie rug from Rug & Kilim anchors the space. The window treatments are fashioned from a Savel textile.

In the primary bath, vintage painted sconces with glass shades illuminate a custom mirror and Grand Brass plumbing fixtures. A series of framed vintage French dried botanical specimens hangs above a vintage blue firkin.

Alan Campbell wallpaper sets the tone in this bedroom, where a vintage bed and console—the latter painted in Benjamin Moore’s Casco Bay—join assorted furnishings from Huniford’s own stock to create a transportive retreat.

In a guest bedroom, twin beds feature headboards covered in a punchy Designtex print and vintage bedding. A side table sourced on Chairish stands beneath a framed collection of 1920s floral prints.

For Huniford, whose primary mission is to understand how all of his clients think and live, the goal here was not to reinvent the family’s lifestyle but to make the house better accommodate it. A windowed banquette in a new bump-out beside the dining table has become a favorite gathering spot; its overhead pottery shelf was inspired by a photograph of decorator and fashion editor Chessy Rayner’s Southampton home. The adjacent sitting room, long a center of family life, was transformed from an awkward triangle into a rectangle, allowing the space to function more comfortably. “Our lifestyle in this house,” the husband now says, “did not change.”

The three-year undertaking benefited from the couple’s willingness to give Huniford considerable creative freedom, and the time to realize his vision. The result feels as though it has evolved over generations rather than been assembled piecemeal, its newfound polish tempered by a familiar sense of ease. “I think a great house should make you feel welcome and welcoming,” says Huniford. And that, it seems, has been the greatest success. As the wife puts it, “Everyone loves to go there.”

Whenever weather permits, the family gathers for meals on the ocean-facing deck, where vintage Brown Jordan chairs with cushions in a Perennials fabric surround a Laurel Group table dressed with a vintage Italian tablecloth, napkins, and tableware.

Huniford’s design extended beyond the architecture and interiors to the surrounding landscape, where the expansive front lawn gave way to meadow grasses, and an asphalt driveway was replaced with gravel. “I’ve done a few gardens for clients before, and I think [these homeowners] understood my sensibility,” says Huniford. “They did not want a lot of maintenance or formal gardens.” The staircase leading to the second-floor entrance ranks among the designer’s favorite structural additions.

#4839. Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin fell below $58,000 Wednesday morning as stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, rising inflation and a fresh round of proposed tariffs from President Donald Trump's administration gave investors more reasons to sell.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.3%, the S&P 500 lost 3%, and Nvidia shed 8.7% as of 9:50 a.m. ET. Bitcoin hit a session low of $57,500 as the selloff on Wall Street spilled over into the crypto market.

Paradoxically, part of the problem is that the U.S. economy is doing better than expected. The Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its estimate of third-quarter GDP growth from 3.4% to 4.3% at an annualized rate, nearly double the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

But the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-over-year in October, up from 3.6% in September and matching a three-year high set in May. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with economists' expectations of 3.2% and September's reading of 3.1%.

“America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told AFP. Consumer spending increased in dollar terms in October but was flat after adjusting for inflation.

A growing economy gives the Fed more room to raise borrowing costs to bring inflation back toward its 2% target. After Wednesday's inflation release, traders were pricing in a 98% probability of a quarter-point increase in December, according to CME FedWatch data. Today odds are set at 94%.

The Fed held rates at between 3.75% and 4% in October after raising them in September for the first time in three years. Traders are also betting on further tightening in 2027, with another increase expected as early as January.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative proposed tariffs targeting 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, following investigations into government policies that encourage manufacturing production beyond market demand.

The proposed rates vary by country and product, with duties of up to 20% on some Chinese imports and up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, subject to adjustments and exemptions. For the EU, the proposed 15% rate accounts for certain existing duties rather than simply adding 15 percentage points to them.

The tariffs have not taken effect, and public hearings are scheduled to begin January 25. If importers pass the additional costs on to consumers, the duties could make the Fed's job of bringing inflation down even harder.

Meanwhile, Wall Street's enthusiasm over Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia didn't last very long. The chipmaker closed Monday up 31.5% but lost more than 6% Tuesday, while Anthropic closed at $81.91, below its $83 initial public offering price less than a week after its Nasdaq debut.

Higher interest rates make it more expensive to finance data centers and reduce the present value of future earnings. Both are particularly relevant for AI companies spending heavily today in anticipation of profits years down the road.

The selloff began well before Wall Street opened. South Korea's Kospi closed 6.16% lower, while spot gold fell 2% to $3,483.59 an ounce by 9:15 a.m. ET, according to Reuters.

Crypto investors were already in bad shape before Wednesday's economic data came out. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported Tuesday that Bitcoin investors were realizing their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX and the subsequent market crash in November 2022, relative to the money that flowed into the asset over the preceding year.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have also recorded $4.94 billion in net outflows this November through Tuesday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, already making it their worst month since launching in January 2024.

The Fed's next interest rate decision is scheduled for December 9.

#4838. Bitcoin sell-off driven by weak demand, forced liquidations: 21Shares

The crypto asset manager warned that Bitcoin’s downturn could persist amid weak investor demand, while forecasting an uneven recovery across crypto sectors.

The $6.4 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance in October triggered Bitcoin’s recent sell-off, but weakening investor demand and forced liquidations drove most of the subsequent losses, according to a Nov. 24 report from crypto asset manager 21Shares.

While the Oct. 29 hack triggered the initial decline, the report found that weakening demand drove Bitcoin (BTC) down a further 8.3% between Nov. 4 and Nov. 11. Forced selling of leveraged positions led to the steepest decline, sending BTC down another 13.5% over the next three days. Crypto liquidations totaled $5.8 billion in the week ending Nov. 15, with long positions accounting for 81%.

Bitcoin’s sell-off and leverage unwind. Source: 21Shares

Signs of weakening demand were also seen in the stablecoin supply, which contracted by $10.7 billion following the hack, marking the largest 18-day decline in dollar terms since the Terra collapse in 2022. US spot Bitcoin and Ether (ETH) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded combined outflows of $3.9 billion between Oct. 30 and Nov. 13.

Eliezer Ndinga, global head of research at 21Shares, told Cointelegraph that the market was already vulnerable before the hack:

The report also found little evidence of selling by other major Bitcoin holders. The 18,270 BTC and 522,409 ETH stolen in the Binance hack remained unspent as of mid-November, while neither the US government nor the Mt. Gox trustee had transferred Bitcoin to exchanges since the attack.

Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy continued buying, adding 2,332 BTC between Oct. 26 and Nov. 15. Meanwhile, miner transfers to exchanges fell to their lowest levels since at least 2020, although the data may not capture sales by publicly traded mining companies.

Related: Bitcoin slides amid US tariff nerves as Anthropic falls below IPO price

21Shares believes Bitcoin is already more than a year into a cyclical bear market. Historically, such downturns have lasted about two and a half years and resulted in average price declines of 84%, according to the report.

However, the researchers see a low probability of Bitcoin revisiting the depths of previous bear markets, citing the growing presence of institutional investors and spot ETFs. Ndinga said the competitive landscape for crypto has also changed:

Ndinga warned that a larger-than-expected Federal Reserve rate hike in December could prolong the downturn. Another potential source of selling pressure is the $2.2 billion in BTC and ETH stolen in the Binance hack, which could reach the market through over-the-counter (OTC) brokers in the coming months.

Ndinga identified Bitcoin’s realized price of $53,250, a measure of the average investor cost basis, as a key downside level to watch. Conversely, a return to the $73,000 to $75,500 range coupled with sustained ETF inflows and rising stablecoin balances would signal renewed investor demand.

Stablecoin supply changes following major market shocks. Source: 21Shares

#4835. Utah moves to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi after trading halt

Utah’s attorney general warned that the criminal charges could be refiled if Kalshi resumes operations in the state, while separate civil litigation remains unresolved.

Utah’s attorney general has moved to dismiss 14 criminal charges against prediction market platform Kalshi and its two co-founders after the company blocked users in the state from accessing its services.

The attorney general’s office said it filed a motion Monday to dismiss the case without prejudice in Utah’s Third District Court, allowing prosecutors to refile the charges if Kalshi resumes operations in the state.

The office opened a criminal investigation into Kalshi in September and filed charges on Oct. 28, alleging that the company offered illegal gambling to Utah residents. Kalshi subsequently agreed to block access to its platform in the state and monitor attempts to reach its services from Utah-based IP addresses.

“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Attorney General Derek Brown said, adding that his office would continue to enforce state gambling laws against other prediction market operators.

The office also sent cease-and-desist letters to several of Kalshi’s competitors, with six other prediction market companies agreeing to stop operating in Utah.

Kalshi General Counsel Yaakov Roth said in a Tuesday post on X that “good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized,” adding that the company was willing to work with state attorneys general while courts resolve the regulatory dispute.

The case is separate from a civil lawsuit Utah brought against Kalshi and its market-making partner Susquehanna International Group on Oct. 20, seeking restitution, damages and the recovery of proceeds from allegedly illegal gambling activities. The complaint estimates that Kalshi collected between $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees from Utah-based accounts as of Oct. 19.

The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced its own lawsuit against Utah on Oct. 27, seeking to block the state from enforcing its gambling laws against federally regulated prediction markets. The lawsuit is part of a broader legal battle over the regulation of prediction markets, with the CFTC asserting exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The federal regulator has sued at least 12 states over the issue.

#4834. Elon Musk’s X Wins Court Judgment Against Alleged Bitcoin Bot Farm Operators

Elon Musk’s X Wins Court Judgment Against Alleged Bitcoin Bot Farm Operators

Elon Musk’s X has won a default judgment in a UK court against two men accused of running a network of Bitcoin-focused accounts that gamed the platform’s creator-payout system, a case that prompted Musk to warn fraudsters: “Don’t mess with X.”

London’s High Court entered the judgment on Nov. 20 against Vivek Kumar Sen and Zamyang Sherpa after neither man filed an acknowledgment of service or a defence, with Master Teverson ruling in favor of X without a trial.

A default judgment means the court entered the order because the defendants failed to engage, not because the allegations were tested and proven. Either defendant can apply within seven days of being served to have the order varied or set aside.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The case dates to a claim issued Sept. 21, when X sued the pair and unidentified accomplices for allegedly operating a coordinated bot army to inflate engagement and siphon money from its Creator Revenue Sharing program.

According to the claim, six enrolled accounts, including handles such as @Vivek4real_ and @Bitcoin_Teddy, were amplified by three additional accounts using likes, reposts and replies to manufacture the engagement that drove payouts.

Crucially, the judgment awards no money yet. Because X sued for “an unspecified sum,” the order states the amount of damages and interest will be decided later at a separate Disposal Hearing.

X has estimated the improperly obtained revenue at no less than £207,384 (about $271,000) and said it is seeking at least £75,000 ($98,000) more in investigation and remediation costs. Those are the company’s claimed figures, not sums the court has granted.

X General Counsel James Burnham announced the ruling, writing that the company had “sued people who abused Creator Revenue Sharing by operating a network of accounts to manipulate engagement” and that the court had now entered judgment against two of them.

“We aren’t kidding around,” he added. “Fraudsters worldwide: Do not mess with X.” Musk reposted the statement with his own terse endorsement.

Even once damages are set, recovering the money is a separate matter that depends on whatever assets Sen and Sherpa hold.

The case reflects the broader strain of the “engagement economy,” where platforms paying creators based on activity have become targets for coordinated manipulation.

X retired Creator Revenue Sharing, which launched in 2023 and paid out based on engagement, on Sept. 7, replacing it the next day with Original Content Rewards, a system it says emphasizes original material over raw engagement volume, a shift partly aimed at the kind of gaming alleged here.

#4833. Europol follows $28.5M crypto trail in streaming piracy crackdown

Authorities from 11 countries worked with Binance, Coinbase and Chainalysis to trace financial transactions and disrupt illegal streaming services.

Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries, working with crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, have traced more than 26 million euros ($28.5 million) in cryptocurrency transactions and disrupted 57 illegal streaming services in an operation coordinated by Europol, the law enforcement agency of the European Union.

In a Tuesday announcement, Europol said the five-day operation took place in Seville, Spain, from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 and identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, attracting more than 7.3 million annual visits combined.

Europol said illegal streaming operators often collect subscription payments in cryptocurrency, allowing them to transfer funds quickly across borders. Investigators traced blockchain transactions to identify links between streaming services, cryptocurrency wallets and the individuals controlling them.

The EU’s law enforcement agency said the operation reflects a shift from focusing solely on shutting down illegal streaming services to also targeting the financial infrastructure behind them. The findings will support ongoing national investigations, including efforts to identify suspects and trace assets linked to criminal activity.

According to figures from the Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance cited by Europol, an estimated 60 million people across Europe use unauthorized internet protocol television (IPTV) services, with estimated annual losses of 4.83 billion euros ($5.3 billion) for legitimate providers and a further 1.08 billion euros ($1.18 billion) in unpaid taxes for governments.

Related: Tron and Tether bring in Chainalysis after T3 crime unit folds

The operation follows other international efforts to disrupt criminal networks and their financial infrastructure. In March, US and European authorities dismantled SocksEscort, a malicious proxy service that enabled crimes including bank fraud and cryptocurrency account takeovers.

The service allowed customers to pay anonymously in cryptocurrency and received at least $5.7 million in user payments, according to investigators. Authorities froze about $3.5 million in cryptocurrency linked to the operation.

Earlier that month, Europol and the FBI took down LeakBase, a cybercrime forum with more than 142,000 registered users. An earlier cybercrime marketplace, RaidForums, had previously hosted leaked personal data belonging to users of crypto hardware wallet provider Ledger.

There’s something downright whimsical about a spindle bed. Its silhouette provides a fairytale-like charm that can make even the most ordinary bedroom feel more enchanting. Its defining feature, the row of slender rods connecting the headboard and footboard, respectively, can take on plenty of personalities, depending on the design. There’s the traditional and ornate bobbin-turned style, as well as the cleaner, more restrained Shaker-inspired and midcentury modern frames. Some spindle beds feel decidedly cottagecore, as if tailor-made for a rustic home nestled in the lush countryside or perched in the highlands; others look right at home in a minimalist space.

Either way, these beds offer an elegant alternative to the sometimes clunky upholstered headboards and lackluster solid-panel frames that can dominate the bedroom. Just see for yourself.

The Mason bed offers a modern interpretation of the spindle silhouette. Oval finials at each corner of the headboard and footboard soften the otherwise industrial feel of its iron frame, while the charcoal powder-coated finish cohesively streamlines the entire piece. Pair it with crisp white percale sheets for a perfectly understated look.

The Jenny Lind bed is a long-held favorite among traditionalists—and for good reason. Its signature bobbin-turned spindles bring a distinctly nostalgic quality to the frame, recalling 19th-century Americana without feeling overly stuck in the past. “While technically a children’s bed, I find that I’m especially comfortable sleeping here at age 28,” says contributor Kate McGregor, who has the bed in black. Solid acacia wood slats provide mattress support, so there's no need for a box spring. Depending on your bedding and surrounding furniture, the design would fit well with a contemporary or totally classic style.

Article takes its cues from Shaker-style furniture with this solid wood bed frame, available in black ash, walnut, and white oak finishes. Its tapered legs and slender spindles give the silhouette a clean, streamlined look that doesn’t feel too plain. The Lenia is also a practical pick for anyone short on bedroom storage, thanks to optional rolling drawers for extra quilts, linens, and the ever-growing collection of things you're simply not ready to part with.

Unlike some of the heavier, more traditional spindle designs, this platform frame has an airy quality that keeps it feeling fresh and decidedly modern. The turned-wood details provide simple yet eye-catching ornamentation. It’s also sturdy, with a solid-wood construction that should stay strong for the long haul.

For a more budget-conscious take on the spindle style, consider this streamlined frame, crafted from solid wood. Its simple spindle headboard nods to midcentury design. With a natural pine finish, it would fit well in a sun-soaked, minimalist space: unfussy, warm, and an exercise in good taste.

With its tapered legs, gently curved lines, and spindle headboard, the Linda bed is a bona fide midcentury staple. The solid wood frame comes in a dark pecan finish that adds just the right amount of warmth. This solid rubberwood frame with matching spindle headboard and footboard designs is available in an impressive collection of finishes. With 26 color options—including a rich green, chocolate brown, and sky blue—possibilities are near-endless for ways to make the bed feel all your own.

Like dumbbells, kettlebells come in a wide range of weights, materials, and grips, so it’s important to determine which type you’re in the market for before you buy.

After testing a handful of kettlebells, this cast-iron option from Amazon Basics earns its spot at the top of our list because of its budget price tag and versatile weight options. The weight range from 10 to 60 pounds has allowed me to ramp up my training intensity over time.

This kettlebell has consistently been my go-to and favorite even as I’ve expanded my collection. They’re surprisingly sturdy and durable, even after two years of use. WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief also loves this model and has multiple in her home gym, too.

I own it in several weight sizes, and it has a compact shape that’s great for every kettlebell exercise imaginable. The grip is slightly textured and wide enough to do one- or two-handed exercises, but petite enough for smaller hands like mine. I can confidently hold it, even during potential wall-breaking moves like swings, and it’s comfortable to hold, whether I’m doing one set or five.

While these weights have a lot going for them, there is one con: There is no vinyl coating on the bottom (although there is a vinyl version, which WH editors also love). To avoid scratching my floors, I have to set it down carefully or use a mat underneath.

Many people prefer a competition-style kettlebell due to its uniform design that’s ideal for high reps and technical moves. The Rep Fitness Adjustable Kettlebell offers a competition-style kettlebell shape with adjustable weights, giving you plenty of space-saving mileage out of one tool.

This kettlebell is well-designed, stacking five weights in one relatively compact design. (Weight ranges include 8 to 16 kilograms, 16 to 24 kilograms, and 20 to 40 pounds.) To adjust the weight, just push down on the dial with two fingers, twist to your desired weight, and lift. It has a rubber base to protect your floors although—heads up—the rubber coating is only there when you use the kettlebell’s full weight. Otherwise, you’ll want to set down your kettlebell gingerly.

REP’s adjustable kettlebell is made from cast iron and feels durable. The textured handle is easy to grip and has plenty of space for two-handed moves, although it feels slightly wider than others. If space is a premium at your place and you’re looking to grow with your kettlebell, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

If you prefer a more traditional competition-style kettlebell, keep scrolling. But if you’re on the hunt for a highly versatile weight that aims to combine the attributes of a kettlebell with those of a dumbbell and a dual-grip medicine ball, the YBell Neo Series is worth consideration.

This weight is perfect for my needs—it’s relatively compact and offers multiple ways to grip, thanks to its unique pyramid-style design. I can use it for everything from biceps curls to lunges, though it’s not ideal for swings.

The grip on this is perfection. It features a neoprene outer layer to create a slightly sticky feel with impressive gripping power, so I’m not stressed about accidentally flinging it across the room during swings. The wide handle leaves enough room for one- or two-handed exercises, but it may feel a little crowded using both mitts at once if your hands are on the larger side.

You have three different spots you can grip on the outside of this weight, along with an inside bar that’s ideal for dumbbell-style work. While the sides are rounded, I found it was relatively easy to rest the YBell on its base or sides to save space.

The only potential downside of this weight is that it tops out at 26 pounds. If you’re interested in doing heavier lifting, you’ll need to upgrade to a different device.

A coated kettlebell like this one from Yes4All protects your floors in case of butterfingers through a thoughtfully wrapped coating up the bottom third of the handle. The handle itself makes for a comfortable grip. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says, “I have the 15-pound model and I never feel it slipping away from me when squatting or doing Russian twists.” It comes in five-pound increments up to 65 pounds, giving you plenty of options.

While I wouldn’t recommend tossing this on your floor at home, the kettlebell doesn’t make a loud noise when it’s dropped, unlike uncoated models. It’s also worth pointing out it’s very affordable, similar to our best overall.Just note the bottom of the kettlebell is not entirely flat, which can be tricky if you’re trying exercises like uneven pushups (with one hand placed through the handles of a KB).

Sand kettlebells are a highly portable option that allows you to add a little more instability to your kettlebell workouts. The GoRuck Sand Kettlebell is built tough thanks to its Cordura nylon design and multiple closure system, so you don’t have to stress about accidentally spilling its contents all over the place.

GoRuck’s kettlebell has a teardrop-style shape that works well for many exercises. This kettlebell arrives empty, so you’ll fill it up with sand prior to use. Pro tip: use playground sand available at home improvement stores for this. The reinforcing on nearly all of the seams and bottoms means you can toss this on the ground without worrying about it flying open and spilling sand everywhere.

This style of kettlebell isn’t for everyone, but if you’re looking to add the extra challenge of sandbag training to your kettlebell workouts, this sand kettlebell design will take a lot of abuse and holds up well over time.

“When choosing the correct weight for your kettlebell, it is important to consider your exercise,” says Almoni Ellis, CSCS, CPT. She says that people generally are able to use heavier weights when doing purely lower-body exercises, but that those weights may be too heavy for a person when they’re doing a move like an overhead press, for example.

That said, there’s no one-size-fits-all starting point. Your experience level and current strength come into play, so if you’re unsure where to begin, try testing different weights at a local gym or consider ordering two sizes to see what feels best. As your strength improves, you can gradually increase the weight, adds Pack.

The most common option for general strength training is the cast-iron kettlebell, which works well for everything from goblet squats to cleans to swings. These are the kettlebells you’ll most often see in home gyms and fitness classes.

Ellis and Pack recommend choosing a cast iron or steel kettlebell because they’re the most durable and long-lasting materials. “Kettlebells [that are] made up of plastic[...] don’t last as long,” Pack says.

However, most adjustable kettlebells are made with some plastic components, which is necessary for the design. As for vinyl-coated kettlebells, they’re usually made of cast iron with a vinyl coating to prevent damage to floors.

Handle thickness plays a role in both comfort and performance. “Thicker handles can help build grip strength, but they may be more challenging for beginners to control,” says Pack.

The handle’s coating and texture matter just as much. A slightly textured surface can help you maintain a secure grip, especially during dynamic or high-rep movements. Slick handles, on the other hand, can become slippery as your hands sweat—raising the risk of losing your grip, Pack adds. If you’re training with kettlebell that has a slick grip, consider using workout chalk or liquid chalk during moves like swings.

To choose the best kettlebells, I consulted three personal trainers who regularly work with kettlebells: Taylor Beebe, CPT, Tyneka Pack, CPT, and Almoni Ellis, CSCS. I also got feedback from Women’s Health fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT, who is a certified trainer.

Based on their feedback, I focused on crucial features to look for in these super versatile strength-training tools. I then tested some of the most popular kettlebells out there. Each was put through a slew of workouts to test its efficiency, durability, weight, material, and grip. Because every person’s budget is different, I made sure to include kettlebells with a range of price points.

#4828. Hackers breach CIA intelligence network in latest US cyberattack

The reported breach follows cyber incidents involving the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and Department of Agriculture.

The US Central Intelligence Agency and at least one other intelligence agency have been hit with a cybersecurity breach that exposed unclassified information, according to The New York Times.

Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Times reported that hackers breached a network used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence that analyzes publicly available information to gather intelligence insights.

It is also believed that other government agencies were exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.

An official with the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. Cointelegraph reached out to the CIA for comment.

The breach adds to a spate of reported cyber incidents at US federal agencies in recent weeks.

The Verge on Tuesday reported the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is also investigating a “cybersecurity incident” that “resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It is not clear if it is related to the recent CIA breach.

Other breaches include the US Department of Agriculture, a leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel records and a hack of the FBI’s national crime database.

Speaking to ABC News about the FBI attack on Sunday, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said cyberattacks have been increasing, and digital infrastructure needs to be upgraded.

“In 2020, there were roughly 750,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI. That’s now up to over a million cyber incidents,” said Clayton.

“And what we’re seeing, though, here, and I want the American people to know this, is we have a step change in technology that we’re facing with superintelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially and we have a dated digital infrastructure.”

Clayton declined to discuss the specifics of the FBI incident but said that cyber incidents were not a new phenomenon.

“Cyber probing, cyber incidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time.”

#4825. CleanSpark weighs selling more Bitcoin than it mines to de-risk books

The Bitcoin miner sold 2,102 BTC while it produced just 1,708 BTC in the September quarter.

Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is considering selling more Bitcoin than it mines each quarter to reduce its treasury risk, according to chief financial officer Gary Vecchiarelli, potentially further drawing down its holdings, last valued at $806 million.

CleanSpark held 13,530 Bitcoin at the end of September after mining 1,708 Bitcoin and selling 2,102 Bitcoin during the quarter, according to Cointelegraph’s tally of the company’s monthly operating updates. It marks the first time since at least 2024 that the company ended the quarter with less Bitcoin than it began with.

During a Q4 earnings call on Tuesday, Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the Bitcoin it mines to cover day-to-day operating costs, and told an analyst that selling slightly more than it produces in a quarter was one way to reduce treasury risk.

“We see the selling of a small amount of Bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of de-risking,” said Vecchiarelli.

“But again, we are going to be sensitive and very reactionary to markets, and we are going to use that capital to make sure that we prevent dilution or bringing additional debt just to grow the company,” he said.

The remarks came as CleanSpark recorded a $987 million net loss for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with a net income of $364 million a year earlier. The company attributed two-thirds of the swing to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings, as Bitcoin’s price fell from about $114,100 to $83,600 over the fiscal year.

Related: Trump-linked American Bitcoin secures $150M credit line from FalconX

CleanSpark also said it sold an undisclosed amount of Bitcoin since September to raise cash for expected acquisitions, as Vecchiarelli said it continues to view its Bitcoin holdings as “a liquid source of non-dilutive capital.”

CleanSpark also cut about 25,000 machines from its Bitcoin mining fleet in the September quarter, bringing the number in operation to about 200,000.

Vecchiarelli said the reduction improved energy efficiency to 14.8 joules per terahash from 15.8 in the previous quarter, which he said should help CleanSpark stay profitable if mining conditions deteriorate ahead of the 2028 Bitcoin halving.

“Going forward, in terms of hash rate, that will probably fluctuate, but we will continue to mine so as long as it’s profitable.”

In Sandersville, Georgia, CleanSpark said its first AI data hall remains on track for the fourth quarter of 2027. CleanSpark said it expects to start unplugging miners at the site in late 2027 as the data center comes online, then decide whether to relocate or sell them.

CleanSpark shares dropped 7.5% on Tuesday ahead of the earnings release to $5.12 and are down 2.25% in after-hours trading.

The company recorded $576.5 million in total revenue in the full year, down 25% from the previous fiscal year. Adjusted EBITDA came in at a loss of $304.2 million for the year.

What Is the Difference Between a Comforter and a Duvet Insert?

A comforter is a single, often quilted, piece of bedding with a fabric cover encasing the doughy fill in between the two fabric layers. A duvet, on the other hand, refers to both the insert and fabric cover. A comforter can be colorful or white, and made in a variety of fabrics. The fabric cover of a comforter is stitched directly onto the fill (down, feathers, or polyester are most common). A duvet’s cover is removable, and often tied to the corners via loops attached to the insert.

Not necessarily. Many duvet inserts are designed to be used on their own, as a comforter, or with a cover. I recommend a cover to help protect your duvet insert, ensure it lasts as long as possible, and make laundry day as easy as possible. Duvet covers act as a protective layer, keeping sweat, body oils, and normal wear from affecting your duvet insert. Plus, duvet covers allow you to add personality to your bedscape, whether you prefer an all-white minimalist look or a maximalist ruffle.

What Is the Best Type of Filling for a Duvet?

Similar to quality, the “best” filling is pretty subjective. People often choose silk, lyocell, down, or down-alternative fills. Down comforters tend to be firmer and heavier, while down-alternatives are usually considered more lightweight and airy. Down-alternatives derive from recycled and allergen-friendly materials, so they’re ideal for people who prefer or require those types of fillings. The fill power will also determine the ultimate comfort level, and most should hover around 650 for a down, cotton candy-like feel.

And again, those care instructions come into play. If you’d rather throw your comforter in the wash, that’s most down comforters in our list can handle it. Meanwhile, some specialty down-alternatives (like bamboo viscose options) need to take a trip to the dry cleaners, which can make them higher maintenance and more expensive long-term.

Does the Quality of a Duvet Insert Matter?

In terms of “quality,” you’ll see the effects in two main areas: the price point and longevity of your duvet insert. For instance, a down comforter with 750 fill power like Brooklinen’s heavyweight comforter is specifically designed for keeping you warm during colder winter months (or for anyone who spends most nights shivering). The fill power makes it lofty and fluffy, but the construction can also keep it lofty and fluffy.

Baffle-box construction, as mentioned above, is also considered a higher quality design option, which holds fill in separate chambers to keep the fill even. All of this said, the most expensive, technically high-quality comforters aren’t necessarily the best for every type of sleeper. And while we love comforters and duvet inserts that run as high as $500, we’ve also scoured the internet and tested alternatives you can shop for less than $100 on Amazon (we’re looking at you, Bedsure Waffle Comforter Set).

It’s also important to keep in mind that your duvet insert’s quality depends on how you care for it. Make sure to carefully read the care instructions, and if needed, take it to a trustworthy dry cleaner for a gentle clean (experts say about two to three times per year).

How Do You Put a Duvet Cover on an Insert or Comforter?

Follow these steps from Monelle Totah, cofounder of Hudson Grace, for a lump-free way to put an insert or comforter inside a duvet cover:

It’s important to always check your specific product’s care instructions before washing. For example, the Buffy Breeze duvet insert recommends a spot clean or dry clean only, while the Boll & Branch comforter is machine washable on a gentle cycle. To take out the guesswork, we’ve included the product’s care instructions right above each of our review descriptions.

Diana Ciechorska, general manager at Park Slope Cleaning, a commercial cleaning company in New York City, says the standard first step for washing your comforter includes treating any visible stains before you load the comforter into the washing machine. “Opt for a gentle cycle with cold water, using a mild detergent,” she says. “An extra rinse cycle ensures no detergent residue remains.”

When taking a comforter out of the dryer, Parima Ijaz, the New Jersey–based founder of bedding line Pure Parima, recommends holding the corners to shake and fluff it. This allows the fill to distribute even after being jumbled up in the dryer. If possible, she says it’s ideal to let the comforter air-dry for an extra day to make sure it is completely dry before dressing your bed.

How Often Should You Wash Your Comforter?

Comforters and duvet inserts accumulate “dust, sweat, and oils, which can cause allergies and wear down the fabric,” says Camden Olivero, COO and cofounder of Clotheslyne, an on-demand pick-up and delivery laundry service. With this in mind, I recommend washing your comforter two to three times a year to help keep allergens at bay and the covering in its best condition (double check the label first, though).

Like your other linens, it’s best to keep your comforter in a cool, dry place to avoid mold or moisture buildup. Keep the comforter out of plastic and cedar too, as these materials can cause yellowing.

If your old comforter is still in good condition, we recommend donating it to charities in your area. However, if you’re looking to purely dispose of old comforters, organizations like Trashie ethically recycle textiles for you to keep them out of landfills—so long as they’re clean and free of soil like motor oil or paint.

What Kind of Duvet Inserts Do Hotels Use?

If you want to mimic your latest hotel stay at home, you’re not alone. We’ve reviewed the best hotel comforters, which are often sold on luxury hotel chain websites like Marriott and Four Seasons. There are several getaways that use Frette’s bedding, too, including The Palace Hotel in Madrid. In most hotel duvet inserts, there are a few common traits: decadent down or hypoallergenic, plant-based down-alternative fills; high fill powers, around 800; organic cotton or bamboo viscose covers for breathability; and carefully designed baffle-box or box-stitch construction to keep fill in place and make it last.

Fortunately, most of our favorite duvet inserts are machine washable and can even go in the dryer. Some will require a commercial washer (especially if they’re bulky), though, and others like the comforters from Quince and Cozy Earth should take a trip to the dry cleaners. Read the care label, and see what’s best for your duvet insert.

Ijaz recommends washing your comforter in a front-loading washing machine since an upright machine is too abrasive. “Using a top loader with a spindle in the middle can damage the comforter and make it harder to properly and evenly wash it,” she says. Otherwise, her general suggestions are like what the experts noted in this story: Wash your comforter on a cold, gentle cycle and avoid harsh softeners and chemicals so the shell and fill stay in the best condition.

How Do I Choose the Right Duvet Insert for Different Seasons?

There are duvet inserts and comforters with heavy fill powers (think 800 and above) for harsh winter months or cold sleepers, lightweight options (400 or below) for summer months or hot sleepers, and medium weights (around 400 to 600) for year-round comfort. We’ve also learned that the fluffiest duvet inserts often give sleepers that Goldilocks-level sleep. “A fluffy, high-loft duvet delivers the most consistent sleep experience across seasons,” Anthony Loiacono, director of rooms at L’Auberge de Sedona, previously told AD. “It provides warmth without weight, and most importantly, adapts to day-to-night temperature shifts.” Frette’s Cortina Medium Down Duvet Filler has all-season appeal, and you can always layer with an extra blanket if you want more coverage on colder nights.

Not all duvet inserts are created equal. This is a lesson you learn early on, when you wake up either sweating or freezing in the middle of the night. The fact is that this annoying experience is also completely avoidable. Reading up on the duvet insert you're considering buying—and actually understanding what all the terms mean—will tell you everything you need to know, including how hot it’s going to be and whether or not the down is going to end up smooshed in one corner come morning. So, I put this guide together with the help of Danielle Trotter, the textiles technical designer at West Elm, to break down what to consider in the confusing world that is duvet insert fillings, fill power, and the different types of construction.

Fill Power: This is the measurement of how much down occupies a cubic inch of space in the insert, a.k.a. how “lofty” it feels. You’ll usually see numbers in the 500s and up. The higher the fill power, the fluffier and warmer it will feel. I typically like fill powers that hover around 800 during the colder months. This fill power is typically on the marshmallowy side of the spectrum and feels cozier and insulating when the temperature outside starts to drop. For the summertime, 600 fill power or so is usually a sweet spot for me since it’s more airy and breathable, but individual preferences may vary.

Corner Loops: If there are corner loops or anchor loops, that means you can use the comforter as a duvet insert. If there are no loops, the comforter might be prone to clumping and bunching within the duvet, so we wouldn’t recommend it unless you have a lot of patience. Some of the loops in this list reach up to 12, which are super helpful to keep the fill even.

Fill Content: Fill material is usually classified as either down or down alternative options.

Outer Shell: The material on the outer shell of your comforter or duvet insert matters. Look at the thread count. I find that fabrics with thread counts around 300 are typically spongy and airy. Consider your preferred sleeping temperature and whether a cotton sateen shell that’s smooth but slightly thicker is a better option than one made of crisp percale cotton. If you’re a hot sleeper, you’ll probably want a cooling material with breathability, like eucalyptus.

Size and Color: The size of your insert is dictated by the size of your bed. Companies usually offer all standard sizes from twin to king, with some brands offering California king as well. In terms of color, white is most popular for the duvet insert, but you can also find ivory relatively easily. Comforter color ranges are more expansive, and you can likely find a hue that fits your decor. I’ve called out what’s available in each of the product picks.

Thread Count: This is the number of horizontal and vertical threads per square inch of the duvet insert's outer fabric. Expert tip: “In theory, people think that the higher the thread count, the better the quality because more yarns are being used,” Trotter says. “However, it’s the quality of the yarns or even the type of weave that really matters!”

Baffle-Box Construction: This design means the comforter or duvet insert has sewn-in square chambers with side walls. “Each chamber has an equal amount of fill, and the side walls prevent the fill from shifting,” says Trotter. “This construction is considered to be of a better quality because warmth is evenly distributed.”

Sewn-Through Construction: This type of construction is when the duvet insert is made of two pieces of fabric sewn around the perimeter, then filled and quilted into squares. This means the top and bottom of the comforter are sewn together. In turn, the fill is shift- and bunch-resistant. While this is a great option for those who like low-maintenance laundry days since you can typically toss these comforter types in the washing machine, the tighter construction usually makes the fill less lofty. Plus, cold air can seep through the seams, so it’s more ideal for a summer bedscape.

#4821. Trump willing to pardon Jensen Huang, says it won’t be necessary

The president’s remarks come days before Jensen Huang is due to face congressional questioning over national security concerns and US chip export controls.

US President Donald Trump has left the door open to pardoning Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, though he said he doesn’t think it’ll be necessary.

Trump made the comments during an interview with the New York Post just a day after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO amid scrutiny over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and whether he allowed the company’s chips to fall into China’s hands.

Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump told The Post: “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Trump had earlier claimed credit for pushing Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back — a move which saw Nvidia’s stock surge on Monday.

Huang is scheduled to testify before lawmakers in a closed-door, transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1.

On Dec. 3, Huang is set to be the sole witness in a hearing by the Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs about US export controls.

#4820. Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gets FCC Approval to Launch AI Data Centers in Space

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites designed to operate as data centers in space, giving Elon Musk the regulatory green light to pursue one of his most ambitious artificial intelligence projects yet.

The constellation, called Starmind, will consist of solar-powered computing modules designed to process large amounts of data in orbit for use back on Earth. It marks the first time the U.S. regulator has authorized a satellite constellation specifically designed for this purpose.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short SpaceX with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

“The Starmind & competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America’s lead in Super Intelligence,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote on X.

“Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk replied.

Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 25, 2026

The FCC even brought a bit of science fiction into its announcement, suggesting the project could bring humanity closer to becoming a Kardashev Type II civilization—a hypothetical society capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star.

SpaceX originally submitted its proposal in January, with the FCC opening a review in February, shortly after Musk folded his AI startup xAI, the developer of Grok, into SpaceX.

Unlike Starlink satellites, which primarily provide internet connectivity, Starmind satellites would perform computations themselves, exchanging information through laser communications. The authorization also allows SpaceX to use radio frequencies as a backup for communications and emergency satellite controls.

Electricity has become one of the biggest bottlenecks in the AI industry. Companies can spend billions of dollars building data centers and buying chips, only to find that local power grids cannot supply enough electricity to run them.

Satellites operating in certain orbits can receive sunlight almost continuously, making solar panels up to eight times more productive than their counterparts on Earth, according to Google research.

Google is pursuing a similar initiative called Project Suncatcher. The company launched its first prototype in October and selected Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company, for another mission scheduled for 2029.

Keeping computers cool in space, despite its reputation for being extremely cold, is surprisingly difficult. The vacuum prevents heat from dissipating through air, meaning satellites need radiators to expel the heat generated by AI chips, which must also withstand exposure to cosmic radiation.

There are environmental concerns, too. The Center for Space Environmentalism warned in September that manufacturing, deploying and eventually deorbiting a constellation of this size could contribute significantly to atmospheric pollution. The FCC said Starmind complies with its orbital debris regulations.

Getting permission to launch a million satellites and actually putting them in orbit are two very different things. During an investment conference earlier this month, Musk estimated that the first Starmind computers could launch in the third quarter of 2027.

SpaceX’s securities disclosures have previously warned investors that its orbital computing business has yet to demonstrate commercial viability and could ultimately prove unsuccessful.
