#4705. Gratitude Works and You Can Make It Work for You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

“Tis the time of year to be grateful (of course), and this might elicit many an eye roll at many Thanksgiving dinner tables. But there’s something to be said about gratitude’s ability to alter our mental and even physical well-being. Before we all tuck into our helpings of turkey this year, here are five surprising benefits gratitude confers, as well as some simple ways to be grateful—even when it feels antithetical to our current state of mind.

People who exhibit more dispositional gratitude have been shown to sleep better. This may be because gratitude, when compared with rumination, is a much more calming way to engage our minds as we wind down. Rumination can ratchet up our emotions and keep us wired. One study found that having individuals with a neuromuscular condition count their blessings each night for three weeks improved their sleep quantity and quality

In a 2016 study, 70 patients with heart failure were randomly assigned either to journal about gratitude for eight weeks or to receive treatment as usual. The researchers found statistically significant reductions in inflammatory biomarkers among participants assigned to the gratitude journal condition. Other studies suggest that gratitude may tamp down inflammation by encouraging prosocial activities, like care and support giving, which can downregulate our body’s stress response.

Both dispositional gratitude and momentary (situational) gratitude can tamp down the green monster of envy, eliminating it altogether or at least morphing it from malicious to benign.

A 2020 study assessed athletic performance across several sports and found that a gratitude workshop enhanced performance, improved stress management, and a more positive attitude towards training. Additional studies have found that gratitude can help protect athletes from burnout and increase motivation on and off the field as a function of hope.

An attitude of gratitude can make or break a marriage or long-term partnership. A 2012 study found that partners who were more appreciative of each other were more likely to respond to one another’s needs, demonstrate more commitment, and engage in more relationship maintenance behaviors, like initiating conflict resolution.

If you’re sold enough on gratitude by the above, here are some ways you can practice it in your everyday life. Even when things feel terrible.

On your morning commute, in your daily shower, or when you’re lying in bed trying to sleep, slowly tabulate as many things as you can in your life at present that are good, neutral, or at least not terrible. This is particularly important if you tend to hold grudges, ruminate over wrongs done to you, or generally focus on the negative. As you do this, you help unhook your attention from the things going wrong in your life and interrupt the rumination cycle.

This classic gratitude exercise entails reflecting at the end of each day on three good things that happened from when you woke to when you sat down to journal or quietly reflect. Even on the worst days, this exercise prompts you to seek at least three good things amid the stress. These things needn’t be enormous or life-changing. They can be as simple as a pretty sunset, a strong cup of coffee, or that you have a roof over your head. Once you’ve come up with three good things, go back to the moments in which you experienced them and reflect in depth on what made them possible, who was involved, and how you felt during them.

Write an email, letter, or record a voice or video note thanking someone who’s done something special for you or someone who just lets you be yourself. Better yet, arrange a "thank you" meet-up over coffee or an activity. The thanks doesn’t have to be for something huge, like saving you from a house fire (though this would certainly be something you would want to thank someone for profusely). It can be for something seemingly insignificant, like checking in on you during a busy time. Be detailed and specific in your thanks. Not just “thanks, that was cool.” But, “I so appreciated how you did _____ because _____; it makes me feel ______.” The more detailed we are in our gratitude, the more (positive) effect it has on the recipient and us.

If you genuinely struggle to see the good in everyday life or you’ve gone through a particularly long stretch of misery, it’s worth reaching out to a mental health professional. What we focus on becomes our reality, and many of us can get caught up in the bad news that seems to be coming at us from every corner of the internet or possibly even our social circles. A therapist can guide you through cognitive behavioral techniques to loosen negativity’s hold on your brain so that you can feel more regulated, safer, and connected—even in an era where that may seem like quite the stretch.

#4704. The Hybrid Training Formula to Run Fast and Lift Heavy

Get the split right, then pick shoes that match the work.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

RUNNING SOMETIMES GETS a bad rap in the weight room, as if a few laps around the block will somehow undo all those hard-earned gains. Turns out, the two activities aren’t the rivals they’re made out to be. Adding miles to your strength routine can build endurance to back up all that muscle. A review study found that combining aerobic exercise with resistance training produced gains in muscle size and maximal strength similar to lifting alone. The benefits work in reverse, too: Smart strength work can also help make you a more efficient runner.

The result? A body that can move serious weight, cover some ground, and handle whatever else you throw at it. Of course, getting the most out of running and lifting takes some strategy, from how you schedule your workouts to how you manage recovery. Another important factor is foot health, which can affect both your big lifts and running splits.

Here’s how to balance running and lifting in your routine, strengthen the feet that support both, and choose shoes for each workout.

YOUR TRAINING SCHEDULE should reflect your priorities. Focused on building strength? Keep your toughest gym sessions front and center and work easy-paced runs around them. Training for a race? Schedule your key runs first. “If your goal is strength, you can’t show up tired,” says Courtney Conley, DC, a chiropractic physician specializing in foot mechanics who recommends separating demanding running and lifting workouts when possible to allow for recovery. Either way, she suggests hitting the weights two to three times a week without going all-out every session.

But if you’re running and strength training, consider also building your explosive power. “You have to train the spring, train that reactive quickness,” Conley says. This is where plyometrics like jumps and hops train you to generate force quickly, absorb impact, and rebound. And, this comes in handy whether you’re sprinting, changing direction on the court, or charging uphill. It will also help your big lifts in the gym, particularly squats, deadlifts, and any type of Olympic lift because it develops things like neuromuscular coordination—allowing you to implement full-body movement patterns and stabilize heavy loads faster; and the rate of force development—how fast you can turn your strength on.

Just make sure you train this way early in your workout, not at the end. “You don’t want to do plyometric training when you’re fatigued,” Conley cautions. Doing so can compromise your form, making those explosive moves less effective and potentially increasing your risk of injury.

THE BODYPART THAT makes all of this training possible is your feet. Their small muscles help you maintain balance, support your arches, and control movement under load. During a squat, for example, those muscles help provide a stable base as you drive through your legs and hips. “Deadlifting is a foot action,” Conley explains. “You’ve got to feel your mid foot and press it into the ground to stabilize your body.”

Running demands just as much. Every stride is essentially a single-leg hop, with your feet and ankles absorbing impact, storing energy, and releasing it to propel you forward. In her practice, Conley sometimes sees clients with weak feet or Achilles issues. “When they go to hop, they sink into the ground, and there’s just no spring out of that system.” It’s one more reason those muscles below your ankles deserve just as much attention as your quads and glutes.

And while you could do specific mobility exercises for your feet, those small muscles get quite a workout when performing single-leg moves that help build strength, balance, and stability.

WHEN YOU TRADE weights for miles, what you need underfoot changes. Your plush running shoes may be great on the road, but they’re no match for the weight room. “When you’re in the gym and you want to lift heavy things, you cannot be wearing your 45 millimeter stack height cushion shoe that has a toe spring on it,” Conley says. “You can’t feel the ground.” For strength training, look for a firm, relatively flat sole that keeps you grounded when the weights get heavy.

One thing to consider is looking for a shoe that allows for balanced weight distribution across the foot. Another is a wide toe-box that allows for your toes to splay. When your big toe has the space to remain straight, it can help keep you stable. It’s this last principle behind the Altra Fit that allows your foot to function naturally: a roomy toe box that gives your toes space while keeping the midfoot secure, rather than making the whole shoe wider. “The widest part of your foot should be your toes,” Conley explains.

And it is this design that can help you choose shoes for running, strength training, or both, that allow your feet to get stronger during all these activities because they support them. “The whole reason I love Altra running shoes so much is because they respect the anatomy of the foot,” Conley says.

Altra offers different cushioning levels, stack heights, and heel-to-toe drops. “If you’re new to this conversation of foot health and strength training, you cannot go zero to 100,” Conley says. In other words, match your shoes to the workout, and if you’re switching to lower-stack or zero-drop footwear, give your feet and calves time to adapt. Here are some Altra shoes to consider:

If you are someone who goes from the weight room to a run (or vice versa), the Escalante 5 keeps things lean with a 24mm stack that has a zero-drop and wide toebox that gives you a stable platform during your heaviest lifts. And for your runs, the responsive EGO cushioning allows you to strengthen your foot with each step no matter whether you are leisurely jogging, crushing speedwork, or doing errands.

If you like to hit the trails with some weight training on the side, the Lone Peak 9 adds a little more cushioning and a grippy MaxTrac outsole for tackling rocky, uneven trails. It also features the Altra’s Original FootShape™ fit and zero-drop platforms that keep your heel and forefoot level.

#4703. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4702. How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 8:49 AM EST

Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

But these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley says samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” says Cowley.

Ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

“You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” says Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) plan to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley says the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into new materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

#4701. 6 Ways You Can Master Intentional 'Life-Crafting'

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In a study published in Frontiers in Psychology, researchers propose a model of “holistic life-crafting,” consisting of six strategies to create a more meaningful life. “Life-crafting” refers to the intentional and proactive process of designing one's life according to personal values, goals, and aspirations.

By intentionally balancing the demands life presents and leveraging available resources, individuals can reshape various facets of life that contribute to meaningful and satisfying living, fostering personal growth and well-being.

Here are six holistic life-crafting strategies to experience more meaning in life, according to the study.

Researchers describe cognitive crafting as a deliberate mindset shift in the way individuals perceive and derive meaning from various aspects of work and life.

Rather than physically changing tasks or circumstances, this strategy involves consciously shifting one’s perspective to initiate change. For instance, if an individual is working long hours and struggles to maintain work-life boundaries, they could begin by cultivating a significant non-work identity and daily practices to mentally disengage from work.

Further, if someone were to lack belief in their abilities, they can practice learning to highlight positive aspects of their work and everyday accomplishments over fretting about what they could not get done. Such alterations in one’s beliefs prompt changes in behavior, better emotional regulation, and a greater sense of control, mastery, and meaning in life.

Another way to create meaningful change is by making external, physical changes to one’s work, home, or other life environments. Environmental crafting often involves setting clear boundaries between different areas of one’s life to prioritize and invest in personally meaningful goals and experiences.

Environmental crafting may include prioritizing time with loved ones or with oneself, engaging in meaningful hobbies, keeping work and living spaces separate, creating a home environment that promotes relaxation and creativity, or surrounding oneself with supportive, positive social connections.

Interest crafting refers to proactively seeking out, cultivating, and immersing oneself in enjoyable activities that hold personal significance and resonate with one's passions and interests.

Researchers suggest that engaging in meaningful activities facilitates the acquisition of new skills, competencies, and access to higher levels of creativity. Witnessing the tangible outcomes of one’s efforts also instills a sense of accomplishment and confidence while serving as a means of rejuvenation and inspiring goal pursuit in other areas of life.

Relational crafting refers to the intentional actions individuals take to maintain significant, fulfilling relationships in their lives. Through discernment, people can decide how to engage, when to engage, and with whom engagement brings the most value and joy. This encompasses not only nurturing positive and energizing relationships but effectively managing emotionally taxing connections.

Research shows that social connections are pivotal in creating and maintaining meaning and mental well-being. Relational crafting also subsumes the skill of navigating social dynamics, including conflict resolution and establishing boundaries essential for sustaining healthy relationships.

Skill crafting involves prioritizing skill development by seeking training opportunities, engaging in challenging projects, and capitalizing on one’s strengths to minimize setbacks.

Its essence lies in aligning one's capabilities with the demands and resources present in the environment. Researchers suggest that individuals who invest in skill crafting often experience heightened confidence, increased self-awareness, and a sense of capability.

Task crafting refers to restructuring daily tasks or life elements in ways that resonate deeply with individuals’ inner drives and aspirations, finding meaning within activities by perceiving them as avenues for personal growth and embracing responsibilities that demand a broader spectrum of skills and competencies.

Researchers suggest that task crafting encourages a more purpose-driven and rewarding life. Individuals can engage in task-crafting by organizing their daily schedule to prioritize personally meaningful, energizing tasks such as going on a walk for their well-being and choosing to invest less time and energy in non-essential tasks such as checking social media excessively.

For instance, allocating specific time slots for checking and responding to emails or scrolling online creates a healthy time boundary between essential and non-essential tasks. This intentional restructuring of the day ensures that individuals invest their energy where it matters most.

Life crafting involves making conscious choices that lead to a more purposeful, balanced, and rewarding life. Individuals can start with introspection, which prompts them to confront limiting beliefs and explore alternative, more empowering perspectives. They must also ask themselves how different spaces in their lives can be altered to better support their needs and align with core values to create a life that is truly meaningful.

#4700. 9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 11:06 AM EST

The Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

They were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially important, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

#4699. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”
